TO: Members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee DATE: January 26, 2026 RE: LD 2008, n Act to Provide Funding to the Maine School of Science and Mathematics and Clarify Sending School Administrative Unit Obligations
My name is Cherie Galyean. I am a resident of Bar Harbor and a parent to a child currently at Maine School of Science and Mathematics. I am writing in support of LD 2008.
My son started at MSSM this year as a sophomore. While he enjoyed his freshman year at our local high school, it became clear that he was not being challenged academically. He came home each day bored with his assignments and frustrated with his fellow students who seemed disinterested in learning.
His first five months at MSSM have been revelatory for all of us. He has absolutely blossomed there. For possibly the first time in his life, he is being appropriately challenged in school. He currently has all As, but he is working extremely hard for them. He has found all his teachers to be supportive and encouraging while upholding a high standard. He enjoys the freedom that dorm life has brought and it has raised his level of independence. While home for winter break, he off-handedly said "I am running low on clothes. I think I'll do some laundry," which possibly marks the first time such a statement has been made by a teenage boy.
As you might expect, I would love to see every child who would like to attend MSSM to be able to do so. By requiring sending districts without a high school to support attendance at MSSM and providing additional funds to students with financial need, LD 2008 would help with this goal. Although my family is able to afford the room and board costs and would not benefit from this assistance, I am keenly aware that the costs would be a barrier for most Maine families. No child should lose out on this high-quality public education because of family finances. Most especially, I strongly support the one-time stipulation for funds for infrastructure upgrades for the MSSM dorms. While the school has done the best it can to steward its buildings, the stress of decades of use is showing.
The truth is that the state has flat-funded MSSM for over a decade--an absolutely untenable situation given inflation and rising student enrollment. Despite their best efforts to stretch their limited dollars, the cracks are beginning to show. This funding is needed to keep MSSM a thriving, positive, challenging place for Maine students like my son. I know that an investment made this year will be paid back at least tenfold with the economic impact these bright, determined, and dedicated students will have on the state.
Thank you for your time and service.

10059036:
Written Testimony
To: Committee On Education and Cultural Affairs
From: Eliza Meyer
Date: 1-29-26
Re: Testimony in Support of An Act to Provide Funding to the Maine School of Science and Mathematics and Clarify Sending School Administrative Unit Obligations
Chair Rafferty, Chair Murphy, and Members of the Committee:
My name is Eliza Meyer, and I am a resident of Vassalboro and the parent of a student at Maine School of Science and Mathematics. I am writing to express my strong support for An Act to Provide Funding to the Maine School of Science and Mathematics and Clarify Sending School Administrative Unit Obligation.
As a parent who has seen my child thrive in the uniquely challenging and supportive learning environment that is MSSM, I am very invested in the success of this school. I also have intimate experience with the confusion that can result when a town that "tuitions out" for secondary school decides that it does not have to contribute towards the cost of attendance at MSSM because the portion not covered by the state is identified as room and board rather than tuition.
The budgetary squeeze that MSSM faces after being flat-funded since FY2017, in combination with increasing costs exacerbated by recent inflation, is very real. The students see it in frequent staff and faculty turnover, aging school infrastructure, and even a reduction in the quality and variety of food in the cafeteria, as the same amount of funding has to somehow cover much higher costs. Parents experience it in watching positions be eliminated or reduced, and when interacting with administration and staff who are doing incredible work but clearly are stretched very thin. I want to be clear that we are not expecting a luxury or elite boarding school experience; we simply want this incredible collection of faculty, administrators, and staff to be able to continue providing an excellent and rewarding learning experience for our students, and to be fairly compensated for their work.
My daughter learned about MSSM from a student in our town who was already attending and became more interested after MSSM was invited to present their program to the eighth graders. Her class was told cost of attendance would be covered like any other public and private school; this did not seem surprising, given that the cost looked similar to the tuition at local high schools, other Maine school districts do cover this cost, and our town had

covered it the last time a student attended. It was only in February of that academic year, after students had worked hard at submitting their applications, we learned that the town would not cover any of the cost of attendance. As you can imagine, this surprised and confused everyone involved, and created a lot of stress for prospective students and their families. After of hours of research, phone calls, emails, meetings, and letter writing over the course of two months, I did some digging through our town's School Board Policies and Procedures; unbeknownst to our current administration and board, our town had a Magnet School Program Policy specifically for MSSM, stating that our town will pay up to the current year local share of the state average tuition rate. This was welcome news, but still left prospective students scrambling to find/confirm funding to cover the remaining $5,000+ within days of the due date for enrollment contracts. Two months of stress and negotiation could have been easily avoided if there were a clear state-wide policy around this issue.
Maine School of Science and Mathematics is an incredible place. Please don't let it die a slow death by attrition, which is a real possibility if funding remains flat. Maine towns have an obligation to provide equitable access to enriched educational opportunities for students who need them; I believe this means that all Maine students should have equitable access to attend the state's only public magnet school, even those students who can't afford to pay the In State cost of attendance. I respectfully urge you to pass this act to ensure that Maine School of Science and Mathematics can continue to provide a worldclass education for Maine's brightest students, and to bring that experience within financial reach of more families.
Thank you very much for your consideration,
Eliza Meyer

Hearing on: LD2008 Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs Testimony: Heather Merriman, Harpswell
January 29, 2026
Honorable Members of the Committee,
Thank you for hearing the important merits of LD2008 before your committee today. I write to you as a grateful graduate of the MSSM and the MSSM Foundation board president.
MSSM is established by, and operates in support of, the Maine Legislature's responsibility to educate our future generation of leaders by providing access to a generative, forward-looking curriculum that is at the forefront of STEM education in the State of Maine. The MSSM Foundation, established even before MSSM opened its doors to the first class of students-has been working tirelessly to raise funds to enhance the education excellence this public program is designed to provide to students experiencing what the Department of Education promises to the children of Maine, a path to "reach their greatest level of achievement."
As we approach the 30th anniversary of the first graduating class, our alumni are now stepping forward. Graduates from our pioneer classes have reached a pivotal moment: after investing years in their own education and careers, they are positioned to give back to the institution that transformed their lives. They are demonstrating their gratitude with financial contributions as well as sharing their expertise, actions that show up in a multitude of ways such as returning to teach at MSSM, supporting the school's specialized programming with their professional experience, or in my case, by volunteering on the Foundation Board, where alumni hold the majority of leadership positions in support of MSSM.
The results speak for themselves. Under this current leadership, the Foundation has achieved remarkable growth. Our program expenditures have increased fivefold--from a three-year average of $33,000 to $190,000 annually. The centerpiece of this growth is the Penguin Fund, an annual giving program that now provides 2% of the school's operating budget.
This is just the beginning; like an exponential curve, the growth in the early evolution of an organization is small. Gratitude for our state's residential magnet school experience is gaining steam. Did you make a gift in support of your public high school last year? I did, and so did my parents. Over 10% of our alumni and their families contributed to the Foundation's fundraising efforts last year--an extraordinary participation rate that reflects the profound impact MSSM has had on their lives. As I settle into my fifth decade of life, I have established my home, family, and career (in environmental engineering) here in my home state. I am grateful that all of the advanced educational opportunities I experienced at the high school and college level were provided at Maine's public institutions.

Page 2 of 2 LD2008
H. Merriman
The Foundation's great strides support only one leg of the stool and without growing support from the legislature, the essential component of the school's funding model (remember this is a school with no municipal tax base contribution, or other mechanism to increase public funds), this school cannot stand. Without state investment, many of our most promising young minds will not receive the special education support they deserve as part of the State's charge to support the full spectrum of learning needs our children represent.
However, private philanthropy cannot do this alone. While the Foundation is confident in our ability to continue growing private support, we cannot replace state investment. The margin of excellence that makes MSSM a nationally recognized institution depends on adequate state funding.
I respectfully urge this Committee to increase state funding for MSSM so that together--through the partnership of public investment and private philanthropy--we can ensure this vital educational resource continues to serve Maine's students and prepare them to contribute to our state's future.
Thank you for your consideration,
Heather Merriman MSSM Class of 1998 Resident of Harpswell

Good day Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and esteemed members of the Committee on
Education and Cultural Affairs. My name is Rob Constantine and I am the current Executive Director of
the Maine School of Science and Mathematics. I am here today for a couple of reasons ~ first to answer any questions you may have on the School's annual report or in general about the state of the School. I recognize that there is a great deal of information in our annual report and that you may not have had a chance to review it thoroughly so I am also happy to return at your convenience to answer those questions
at another time.
Second, I would like to express my support for LD2008 and share some of the lived experience on
campus that this bill would address. LD2008 addresses three on-going challenges at the School - a lack of clarity around responsibilities of full school choice districts, a funding model that has resulted in static
operating funding for 9 years, and deferred maintenance of state facilities as a result of that flat funding.
Current statute lays out expectations of full choice sending school districts for just about every case they
could face. . .except MSSM. Title 20A, Section 5 805 includes specific direction on tuition calculation for other public schools and private schools. It specifically mentions MSSM. . .but provides no guidance for
calculating sending district responsibility. While some districts do pay toward the costs of attending
MSSM, others pay nothing. It is a little embarrassing that I was able to receive tuition fi'om sending
Maine towns when I worked at a private school in NH. . .but sometimes do not as the director of Maine's public magnet school. This past admission cycle we worked with a family in a sending district that at first
indicated they wouldn't pay anything toward MSSM (though they would have paid an even higher
amount for the student to attend a nearby private school). This was late in the cycle after all of our available financial aid funds were allocated. While the district's school board eventually made the decision to pay, the lack of clarity created a great deal of confusion and stress for the family.
Throughout my tenure I have come before you to share the success of our students and the challenges of
flat-funding. Each year of flat funding actually represents a decreased state's investment in MSSM when
the impacts of inflation are taken into account. The request for additional financial aid funds and on- going
operating funding are not desired additions - let me be clear that they are merely a way for the state to

TESTIMONY NEITHER FOR NOR AGAINST
L.D. 2008
AN ACT TO PROVIDE FUNDING TO THE MAINE SCHOOL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS AND CLARIFY SENDING SCHOOL ADMINISTRATIVE UNIT OBLIGATIONS
January 29, 2026
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, I am Robbie Feinberg, Director of Communications and Government Relations for Maine School Management Association, testifying on behalf of the legislative committees of the Maine School Boards Association and Maine School Superintendents Association regarding L.D. 2008, An Act to Provide Funding to the Maine School of Science and Mathematics and Clarify Sending School Administrative Unit Obligations.
Maine's school leaders recognize the important role that MSSM plays as Maine's only public magnet school, providing opportunities for students to be challenged academically and pursue their varied interests. MSSM operates differently than the rest of Maine's public education system with its admissions structure and residential model, and we respect that it offers a unique atmosphere that has benefited Maine students and families.
Our associations also recognize what could be perceived as a current inequity in Maine law:
� If a student from a district without its own high school sought to attend a local private or independent school, the district would be required to pay a portion of the tuition cost
� However, if that same student chose to attend MSSM, MSSM would not receive that same tuition payment
This bill seeks to address that seeming inequity, and our associations respect the bill's attempt to resolve it.
Our only concerns regarding this bill are the uncertain financial impact that it could place on certain Maine districts. Many Maine communities already help to pay for a student's room and board if they attend MSSM, but they are not required in law. This bill would mandate it and potentially add new costs onto certain districts at a time when schools across Maine face challenging budget pictures.
L.D. 2008 also creates different monetary obligations for a school district, depending upon whether or not the district has its own high school. Only particular districts - those that do not operate or contract with a secondary school - would have this new monetary obligation, potentially raising questions of fairness and equity.
Because of these questions, our associations are neither for nor against this bill.
